paragraphs: The paper studies how to separate a large data matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse component. The low-rank part represents structure that can be described using relatively few independent directions. Conventional decomposition methods have a computational cost proportional to both matrix dimensions and the rank, which can become prohibitive for large datasets.

The proposed randomized method learns the relevant subspace from a small selection of columns and rows, then uses that information to recover the low-rank component. Its stated complexity is O(max(N₁, N₂)r²), compared with O(N₁N₂r) for conventional methods. This changes how the computational burden grows with matrix size.

The sampling analysis also explains when a small selection is sufficient. Even with uniform random sampling, roughly O(rμ) columns or rows suffice, where μ is the low-rank component’s coherence parameter. This is a sufficient sampling result, not a universal minimum. The paper additionally develops sampling algorithms for structured data, addressing cases where uniform sampling may use observations inefficiently.
icml-2016-a-subspace-learning-approach-f.tldr: Learning a low-rank subspace from selected rows and columns reduces the stated cost of large matrix decomposition.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the dynamic memory network, an architecture that treats language tasks as answering questions about an input. It processes both the input sequence and a question, builds episodic memories, and produces an answer. The motivation is that many language problems can share this input-question-answer structure despite asking for different kinds of outputs.

Its central mechanism is repeated, question-directed attention. Each pass can depend on the input and on what earlier passes have already produced. This lets the network revisit information with an updated internal context. A hierarchical recurrent sequence model reasons over the resulting memories to generate the answer, and the full architecture can be trained together.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on the stated evaluations: bAbI question answering, Stanford Sentiment Treebank sentiment classification, and WSJ-PTB part-of-speech tagging. Training across these tasks uses learned word vectors and input-question-answer triplets. These findings support the usefulness of a shared memory-and-attention architecture across several language tasks, without establishing that every language problem fits equally well.
icml-2016-ask-me-anything-dynamic-memory.tldr: Dynamic memory networks use repeated question-directed attention to support several language tasks within one trainable architecture.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a measurement problem in reinforcement learning: progress in continuous control was difficult to assess without a commonly adopted benchmark. Continuous control involves choosing actions from a range of possible values. The contribution is a shared collection of tasks and algorithm implementations that makes systematic evaluation easier.

The suite deliberately includes different sources of difficulty. It covers familiar tasks such as cart-pole swing-up and problems with large state and action spaces, including three-dimensional humanoid locomotion. It also includes tasks with partial observations and hierarchical structure. Together, these settings allow evaluation to extend beyond a single kind of control problem.

The authors systematically evaluate a range of implemented reinforcement learning algorithms and report findings from those comparisons. They release both the benchmark and reference implementations to support reproducibility and broader adoption. The stated contribution therefore combines experimental evaluation with reusable research infrastructure: other researchers can work from shared tasks and implementations when assessing their own methods.
icml-2016-benchmarking-deep-reinforcemen.tldr: A shared continuous-control benchmark and reference implementations support more systematic, reproducible reinforcement learning comparisons.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks support exact probabilistic inference in time proportional to network size, but learning their parameters presents a different computational problem. The paper explains that maximum-likelihood training can overfit compared with Bayesian approaches. Yet exact Bayesian posterior inference is intractable, so obtaining the benefits of Bayesian learning is not straightforward.

Standard approximation methods also face difficulties because each data instance introduces many local latent variables. According to the abstract, this makes ordinary variational inference and posterior sampling computationally infeasible even for moderately sized networks. The proposed solution is a deterministic collapsed variational inference algorithm designed specifically for sum-product networks.

The method offers an efficient optimization formulation that can incorporate prior information and is described as easy to implement. Experiments show a significant accuracy improvement over a maximum-likelihood approach. The result matters because it connects a practical training procedure with the ability to use prior information, while preserving the distinction between efficient inference in an existing network and the harder task of Bayesian parameter learning.
icml-2016-collapsed-variational-inferenc.tldr: Collapsed variational inference makes Bayesian-style parameter learning practical for sum-product networks and improves reported accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies exploration when an organization must keep performance above a fixed baseline throughout learning. A company may want to try new revenue-generating strategies, but cannot simply accept poor interim performance in exchange for a good final outcome. This produces a stricter bandit problem than requiring the revenue constraint only at one future time.

The authors develop strategies for both stochastic and adversarial settings and analyze the cost of maintaining the constraint. Their results distinguish guarantees that hold in expectation from guarantees that hold with high probability. They make this distinction for both regret, which measures the cost of learning relative to a comparison strategy, and satisfaction of the revenue constraint.

A lower bound shows that the stochastic algorithm is almost optimal. In the adversarial setting, maintaining the constraint appears more expensive, at least for the algorithm studied; this is not stated as a universal separation. Experiments in synthetic environments complement the theory. The work makes ongoing performance requirements an explicit part of exploration rather than an end-of-training check.
icml-2016-conservative-bandits-ce8547bdc.tldr: Conservative bandit algorithms explore new options while maintaining a baseline performance constraint throughout learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions in which an agent chooses an ordered list but observes outcomes only until a stopping event. A recommendation list may stop yielding feedback at the first selected item; a route may reveal outcomes only as far as the first blocked edge. The agent also receives contextual information before choosing the list.

The model incorporates position discounts, so the reward depends on where the stopping event occurs. Ordering therefore affects more than which items are presented: it also affects how their outcomes contribute to reward. The authors combine contextual information, list selection, partial feedback, and position-dependent rewards in a broader cascading bandit formulation.

They propose C³-UCB, an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds, and prove a general regret bound growing as the square root of the number of steps, up to logarithmic factors. They also provide finer analyses for two special cases. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate advantages from including context and position discounts, supporting the value of representing both in the learning problem.
icml-2016-contextual-combinatorial-casca.tldr: C³-UCB learns ordered lists using context, position-dependent rewards, and feedback that stops partway through the list.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning from comparisons between pairs of options rather than observing a separate reward for each option. Its target is a Copeland winner: an option that beats the greatest number of other options. This defines success through the pattern of pairwise wins, making the problem one of discovering which comparisons matter for identifying strong candidates.

The authors characterize the difficulty through an asymptotic regret lower bound and introduce CW-RMED, an algorithm with an asymptotically optimal regret guarantee. Here, asymptotic optimality concerns behavior as learning continues. It does not settle the practical cost of choosing the algorithm’s next comparison, and the abstract explicitly leaves its efficient computability unresolved.

To address that issue, the paper develops ECW-RMED, a computationally efficient version, and derives an asymptotic regret bound for it. Experiments show that this version significantly outperforms existing dueling bandit algorithms in the reported comparisons. The contribution separates the best achievable learning performance from the computational challenge of implementing a strategy that pursues it.
icml-2016-copeland-dueling-bandit-proble.tldr: The paper establishes asymptotic limits for Copeland dueling bandits and develops both an optimal algorithm and an efficient variant.

paragraphs: This paper brings cumulative prospect theory into risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. CPT evaluates uncertain outcomes using distorted probabilities and is motivated by evidence about human decisions. It is more general than the expected-utility and coherent-risk formulations discussed in the abstract, allowing the learning objective to reflect a different treatment of uncertainty.

Applying CPT introduces two challenges: estimating the objective requires information about the entire value distribution, and control involves finding a randomized optimal policy. The authors first develop an estimator that uses an empirical distribution to calculate the CPT value of a random variable. This makes distributional estimation a direct component of the learning procedure.

They then place that estimator inside an optimization loop based on simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation, a simulation-based optimization method. The paper supplies convergence guarantees for all proposed algorithms and empirical demonstrations of their usefulness. Its contribution links prediction and control through the same CPT estimator, providing a route from evaluating uncertain returns to optimizing behavior under that evaluation.
icml-2016-cumulative-prospect-theory-mee.tldr: The paper develops convergent estimation and control algorithms for reinforcement learning objectives based on cumulative prospect theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies ranking when users can click several items before finding something satisfactory. In its dependent click model, a user examines a list in order, clicks attractive items, and stops when satisfied. The learning objective is to increase the probability of recommending satisfactory items, which is different from merely collecting clicks.

The central difficulty is that the learner does not observe which attractive item actually satisfied the user. The authors formulate an online learning problem around this incomplete feedback and propose dcmKL-UCB, a computationally efficient algorithm. They derive regret upper bounds that depend on performance gaps under stated reasonable assumptions, along with a lower bound matching up to logarithmic factors.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show good performance, including cases where the assumed click model is misspecified. That robustness is an empirical finding rather than a guarantee for arbitrary user behavior. The work presents a practical, regret-optimal approach to learning rankings with multiple clicks within a cascade-like model, connecting a richer interaction model to learning guarantees.
icml-2016-dcm-bandits-learning-to-rank-w.tldr: DCM bandits learn rankings from multiple clicks while accounting for the unobserved distinction between attractiveness and satisfaction.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear bandit learning across a peer-to-peer network whose members have limited communication. The aim is to let peers benefit from shared experience without assuming that every observation can immediately reach a central learner. The authors propose two distributed algorithms based on confidence balls, which represent uncertainty in the learning problem.

The first algorithm assumes that every peer is solving the same linear bandit problem. Under that assumption, its asymptotic regret rate matches the optimal rate available to a centralized algorithm with instantaneous communication. This is a statement about the rate of learning over time, rather than a claim that communication limitations have no effect at every stage.

The second algorithm allows different clusters of peers to face different problems, while peers inside each cluster share a problem. It discovers these clusters and achieves the optimal asymptotic regret rate within each one. Experiments on several real-world datasets compare the methods with the state of the art. The distinction between the algorithms makes the assumed pattern of shared problems explicit.
icml-2016-distributed-clustering-of-line.tldr: Distributed linear bandit algorithms achieve optimal asymptotic regret rates while sharing limited information and, when needed, discovering peer clusters.

paragraphs: The paper develops conditional generative models for learning the temporal dependencies of multiple sequences together. It builds on temporal sigmoid belief networks, which arrange sigmoid belief networks across time. The goal includes both understanding sequential data and generating sequences whose characteristics can be influenced by additional information.

A three-way weight tensor models multiplicative interactions between side information and the sequences. This gives side information a role in shaping the modeled temporal relationships. The authors then factor the transition matrices to reduce the number of parameters and improve generalization. These two design choices combine a richer form of conditioning with a more economical parameterization.

The paper also provides a semi-supervised framework for settings where side information is unavailable, supporting robust sequence classification. Experiments report state-of-the-art predictive and classification performance on the sequential data studied. The model can also synthesize sequences with controlled transitions and blends between styles. These findings connect its conditional design to both predictive tasks and controllable generation, rather than treating generation as its only purpose.
icml-2016-factored-temporal-sigmoid-beli.tldr: Factored temporal sigmoid belief networks combine side information with sequence dynamics for prediction, classification, and controllable generation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses position bias in crowdsourced ranking: some annotators may respond partly to where an option appears, potentially degrading the final consensus labels. Collecting many annotations cheaply does not by itself resolve this problem. The authors develop a statistical framework for modeling and detecting this particular form of abnormal annotation behavior.

The framework controls the false discovery rate without requiring advance knowledge of how many annotators are biased. This targets the expected fraction of incorrect flags among all flagged annotators. It therefore evaluates the reliability of the collection of discoveries, rather than promising that each individual flag must be correct.

The technical approach adapts knockoff filters and introduces algorithms based on inverse scale space dynamics. Their discretization is described as potentially suitable for large-scale crowdsourcing analysis, preserving a distinction between proposed scalability and an unconditional scalability guarantee. Experiments with simulated and real-world data support the approach. The resulting tool makes annotator assessment quantitative while explicitly accounting for false accusations of position bias.
icml-2016-false-discovery-rate-control-a.tldr: A statistical framework detects position-biased annotators while controlling the expected proportion of false discoveries.

paragraphs: This paper frames personalized summarization as choosing a useful subset of data under several user constraints. Its utility functions satisfy diminishing returns: an item can add less value when much relevant material is already selected. The formulation also permits nonmonotone utility, so adding an item need not always improve the summary.

The proposed FANTOM algorithm handles the intersection of a p-system and multiple knapsack constraints. In the summarization application, the p-system can represent selection rules involving categories or timestamps, while knapsacks express limits such as budget or time. The algorithm comes with an approximation guarantee and a bound on the number of utility queries, making both solution quality and computational effort part of the analysis.

The authors evaluate movie recommendation over 11,000 movies, personalized summarization of 10,000 images, and revenue maximization involving 5,000 YouTube communities. FANTOM consistently achieves the highest utility among the baselines in those experiments. These results support its practical use for constrained selection across several applications, while the theoretical formulation explains how diverse user requirements can fit into one optimization problem.
icml-2016-fast-constrained-submodular-ma.tldr: FANTOM efficiently selects high-utility summaries while accommodating category rules, budgets, and other simultaneous constraints.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a network can optimize a shared objective when data are spread across its nodes. Its focus is on pairwise functions, whose terms involve relationships between data points. This structure appears in ranking, distance metric learning, and graph inference, making coordination relevant to the objective itself as well as to communication.

The authors propose gossip algorithms based on dual averaging. Nodes communicate according to the network’s graph, and the framework supports both synchronous and asynchronous operation. It also accommodates constrained and regularized optimization, so the shared learning problem can include restrictions on solutions or penalties within the objective.

The theoretical result preserves the convergence rate of centralized dual averaging up to an additive bias term. That qualification matters: the analysis does not claim complete equivalence to centralized computation. Numerical simulations on area-under-the-ROC-curve maximization and metric learning illustrate practical value. Together, the analysis and simulations show how decentralized communication can support objectives built from pairs of observations while making the remaining bias explicit.
icml-2016-gossip-dual-averaging-for-dece.tldr: Gossip-based dual averaging optimizes distributed pairwise objectives with centralized convergence rates up to an additive bias term.

paragraphs: This paper studies k-means clustering when different dimensions of the data reside on different machines. Each machine therefore holds only part of the feature description needed for clustering. The central challenge is to coordinate a useful clustering solution while keeping the amount of information exchanged between machines low.

The authors provide approximation algorithms with constant approximation ratios and low communication costs. A constant ratio bounds solution quality relative to the optimal clustering objective, rather than requiring exact optimization. The stated communication complexity significantly improves on existing algorithms, connecting a guarantee about clustering quality with a guarantee about the cost of distributed coordination.

The paper also establishes a communication lower bound that nearly matches its upper bound within a particular range of parameter settings. This identifies a regime where the algorithms’ communication requirements are close to unavoidable, without claiming that conclusion for every regime. Experiments on real datasets show the proposed algorithms outperforming existing methods in the distributed-dimension setting, complementing the theoretical analysis.
icml-2016-k-means-clustering-with-distri.tldr: New k-means approximation algorithms reduce communication when data features are split across machines.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a video classification model that combines a convolutional neural network with a temporal pooling layer. The layer converts information from a video sequence into a vector of fixed length while encoding temporal semantics. This addresses the need to represent clips of different lengths in a form that a common classifier can use.

The temporal representation is produced through an inner optimization problem. Training the overall model is then formulated as bilevel optimization: the representation-producing optimization sits inside the larger learning problem. This arrangement allows the representation and classification parameters to be learned jointly, so temporal summarization participates directly in end-to-end training.

The approach supports arbitrarily long clips and can use existing convolutional architectures, including AlexNet or VGG, without modifying them or introducing additional parameters. The authors demonstrate it on action and activity recognition tasks. Its significance lies in making an optimization-based temporal summary compatible with joint learning, while retaining existing convolutional architectures as the foundation for the video model.
icml-2016-learning-end-to-end-video-clas.tldr: An optimization-based temporal pooling layer lets video representations and classifiers learn jointly from variable-length clips.

paragraphs: The paper examines inference in dynamical systems, where observations arrive over time and a learner must maintain useful information for filtering or prediction. Traditional latent state-space models first learn an underlying hidden-state model and then use it to perform inference. The authors identify both learning difficulty and a lack of inference guarantees as concerns with that route.

Their predictive state inference machine, or PSIM, learns the inference procedure directly. It treats that procedure as a composition of predictors operating in predictive state space. This shifts the learning target toward the sequence of predictions needed for inference, rather than making inference depend on first recovering a separate latent-state model.

The paper provides theoretical inference guarantees in both realizable settings and agnostic settings. These cover the distinction between a setting where the chosen model class can represent the target and one where an exact match need not exist. Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotics benchmarks showcase practical performance. The contribution combines a direct learning formulation with theory aimed at the inference task itself.
icml-2016-learning-to-filter-with-predic.tldr: PSIM learns dynamical-system inference directly as a composition of predictors and supplies guarantees for that inference.

paragraphs: This paper adds external memory to a deep generative model to address information lost during representation learning. Extracting high-level, invariant features can discard local details that matter when generating an individual example. The proposed model uses attention over a potentially large memory to capture that detail information alongside its more abstract representation.

A smooth attention mechanism allows the network to be trained end to end. Training optimizes a variational bound on data likelihood through auto-encoding variational Bayesian methods. An asymmetric recognition network is learned jointly to infer high-level representations. The architectural asymmetry can reduce competition between extracting invariant features from observations and reconstructing instance-specific detail during generation.

Experiments on several datasets report significant benefits from memory for density estimation, image generation, and missing-value imputation. The authors also report state-of-the-art quantitative results for generative models with memory. These findings support external memory as a useful complement to learned abstractions: the model can use a high-level representation while also having a mechanism dedicated to information that abstraction may lose.
icml-2016-learning-to-generate-with-memo.tldr: An attention-based external memory helps deep generative models retain local details alongside high-level representations.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search uses simulated outcomes to guide planning, and its backup strategy determines how those outcomes update values within the search tree. This paper focuses on that update process. It asks whether more complex return strategies from reinforcement learning can improve planning compared with backing up values through Monte Carlo averaging.

The authors transfer these strategies into tree search and construct four new variants. On some probabilistic planning benchmarks from the International Planning Competition, choosing a variant with a different backup strategy produces substantially better results. The qualification is central: the finding concerns particular benchmark environments, rather than identifying one backup strategy as uniformly best.

The paper also proposes a hypothesis explaining why backup strategies perform differently across environments. To investigate it, the authors manipulate a carefully structured grid-world and obtain empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis. This adds an explanatory component to the comparisons, connecting the choice of value update to environmental characteristics and showing that backup design can materially affect search performance.
icml-2016-on-the-analysis-of-complex-bac.tldr: Alternative value-backup strategies substantially improve Monte Carlo tree search on some planning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Many sparse learning problems are naturally expressed as nonconvex optimization, motivating the use of more tractable convex relaxations. This paper asks what statistical accuracy can be lost through that choice. It studies mean estimation for a sparse principal submatrix and edge-probability estimation for a stochastic block model.

The analysis uses the sum-of-squares hierarchy to characterize the limits of a broad class of convex relaxations. In the problems examined, achieving computational tractability through these relaxations requires compromising statistical optimality. The result therefore concerns the relationship between an optimization approach and the accuracy it can attain, rather than only the time needed to solve its optimization problem.

A distinguishing feature is that the theory does not depend on unproven computational-hardness assumptions. Other lower-bound approaches discussed in the abstract address general polynomial-time algorithms using hypotheses about problems such as planted clique detection. Here, the scope is narrower—a broad class of convex relaxations—but the conclusions within that scope avoid those hypotheses. This provides a different form of evidence for a computation–accuracy tradeoff.
icml-2016-on-the-statistical-limits-of-c.tldr: The paper proves statistical limits for a broad class of tractable convex relaxations without relying on unproven hardness assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper focuses on solving ridge regression more quickly. Its contribution is a preconditioning method based on linear sketching, combined with stochastic variance reduced gradient, or SVRG. The target remains the ridge regression problem; the new method changes how the solver is equipped to approach that problem.

Preconditioning serves as a preparation step for optimization, and linear sketching supplies the basis for constructing that preparation. The proposed combination therefore has two distinct components: a sketch-based preconditioner and the SVRG optimization procedure that uses it. This arrangement matters because the contribution is not simply another use of SVRG; it modifies the conditions under which SVRG performs its work.

The abstract reports a significant speed-up relative to fast stochastic methods, specifically SVRG, SDCA, and SAG. Including SVRG itself among the comparisons makes the benefit of adding the preconditioning process especially relevant to the stated result. The paper’s central finding is thus computational: combining sketch-based preparation with an established stochastic solver can substantially accelerate ridge regression.
icml-2016-solving-ridge-regression-using.tldr: A linear-sketching-based preconditioner significantly accelerates SVRG for ridge regression relative to several fast stochastic solvers.

paragraphs: This paper proposes design principles for recurrent neural networks inspired by physics and functional programming. Its type constraints play a role analogous to dimensional rules that prevent adding incompatible quantities such as meters and seconds. The goal is to guide architecture design through meaningful restrictions rather than relying only on searches over increasingly complicated structures.

The architecture separates stateless learned computation, called learnware, from state-dependent computation, called firmware. This factorization is intended to reduce the impact of side effects. The resulting learned features have an interpretation as dynamic average pooling over one-dimensional convolutions, giving the network’s sequence processing a more explicit semantic description.

The authors show that gradients in strongly typed networks are better behaved than those in classical architectures and characterize their representational power. Experiments find lower training error and comparable generalization error despite the additional constraints. These findings suggest that structured restrictions can coexist with effective learning. They also distinguish improved training performance from generalization, for which the reported result is comparability rather than superiority.
icml-2016-strongly-typed-recurrent-neura.tldr: Strong typing imposes interpretable structure on recurrent networks while yielding better-behaved gradients and competitive experimental performance.

paragraphs: This paper accelerates texture synthesis and artistic style transfer by moving expensive computation into a learning stage. The earlier approach discussed in the abstract generates images through a slow, memory-intensive optimization process. Here, a compact convolutional network is trained so that producing an image can subsequently use a feed-forward computation.

Given a single texture example, the trained network can generate multiple samples of that texture at arbitrary sizes. The approach also supports transferring the artistic style of a given image to other images. Training therefore constructs a reusable generator, allowing the learned computation to serve repeated synthesis requests.

The authors report texture quality comparable to the earlier method while generating textures hundreds of times faster. This speed claim concerns generation with the resulting networks, consistent with shifting work to training. More broadly, the paper demonstrates the usefulness of training feed-forward generative models with complex, expressive loss functions: an elaborate training objective can lead to a lightweight model for producing outputs.
icml-2016-texture-networks-feed-forward-.tldr: Compact trained networks generate textures of comparable quality to an optimization-based method hundreds of times faster.

paragraphs: The paper connects the generalization of stochastic gradient methods to algorithmic stability: how sensitive training is to changes in the data. It shows that parametric models trained with sufficiently few iterations have vanishing generalization error under the analysis. This makes training duration relevant to statistical behavior as well as computational expense.

The authors derive stability bounds for both convex and nonconvex optimization using elementary tools from convex and continuous optimization. Their results rely on standard Lipschitz and smoothness assumptions. These conditions and the role of iteration count are part of the claim, so the result does not say that every short training run automatically produces an accurate model.

For convex problems, the analysis offers insight into why multiple training epochs can still generalize well. For nonconvex problems, it provides a stability-based interpretation of common neural-network practices and formally identifies popular training techniques as stability-promoting. The contribution explains one route by which optimization choices influence the gap between training behavior and performance beyond the training data.
icml-2016-train-faster-generalize-better.tldr: Stability analysis explains how stochastic gradient training duration and common training practices can support generalization.

paragraphs: Frank–Wolfe optimization is useful for structured constraints because it avoids projection steps. This paper develops its stochastic form, where optimization relies on stochastic gradient information. The authors introduce two variants that use variance reduction to improve the number of gradient evaluations required to reach the stated accuracy target.

The improvements depend on properties of the objective. For smooth, strongly convex objectives, the reported gradient-evaluation requirement improves from O(1/ε) to O(log(1/ε)). For smooth, Lipschitz objectives, it improves from O(1/ε²) to O(1/ε^1.5). These are conditional complexity results, and they concern stochastic gradient evaluations rather than an unconditional statement about every component of running time.

Experiments on real-world datasets for multiclass classification also exhibit the theoretical improvement. The contribution connects the projection-free handling of constraints with more efficient use of stochastic gradient information. That combination matters because retaining a useful constraint-handling strategy need not mean accepting the previously reported gradient-evaluation costs in the settings covered by the analysis.
icml-2016-variance-reduced-and-projectio.tldr: Variance reduction lowers stochastic gradient-evaluation requirements for two projection-free Frank–Wolfe variants under stated objective assumptions.
